content: If a research participant suffers an injury or disability as a result of their participation, they are entitled to compensation. In the event of death caused by their involvement in the research, their dependents are also entitled to compensation. Participants must not be asked to waive their right to such compensation. Guideline 20: Strengthening Capacity for Ethical and Scientific Review and Biomedical Research Many countries lack the infrastructure or expertise to evaluate the scientific quality or ethical acceptability of biomedical research conducted within their jurisdictions. In cases of externally sponsored collaborative research, sponsors and investigators have an ethical responsibility to ensure that the research projects they oversee contribute meaningfully to the development of national or local capacity. This includes the ability to design and conduct biomedical research, as well as to provide scientific and ethical review and monitoring of such research. Capacity-building efforts may involve activities such as: Establishing and enhancing independent and competent ethical review processes or committees. Strengthening research capacity. Developing technologies tailored to healthcare and biomedical research needs. Training research and healthcare personnel. Educating the community from which research participants will be recruited. Guideline 21: Ethical Obligation of External Sponsors to Provide Health-Care Services External sponsors are ethically obligated to ensure the availability of: Health-care services essential for the safe conduct of the research. Treatment for participants who experience injuries as a result of research interventions. Services necessary to fulfill the sponsor’s commitment to make beneficial interventions or products developed through the research reasonably accessible to the population or community concerned. Annex 3: Searching the Literature 1. The US National Library of Medicine (NLM) The US National Library of Medicine is the largest biomedical library in the world. Since 1879, it has indexed biomedical literature to provide health professionals with access to information essential for research, healthcare, and education. NLM offers a vast and frequently updated database called MEDLINE. MEDLINE MEDLINE is NLM’s premier bibliographic database, covering fields such as medicine, nursing, dentistry, veterinary medicine, and pre-clinical sciences. It has been available for online searching since 1971, effectively replacing the printed Index Medicus. Advantages of online searching include rapid retrieval, access to more journals, availability of abstracts, and the ability to search by non-MeSH terms in titles and abstracts. MEDLINE includes over 12 million records dating back to 1966, with approximately 40,000 new citations added monthly. PubMed PubMed provides access to MEDLINE and additional citations, including those predating a journal’s inclusion in MEDLINE. It also links to PubMed Central, an archive of life sciences journals offering free full-text access to over 100,000 articles from more than 130 journals. MeSH (Medical Subject Headings) MeSH is NLM’s controlled vocabulary for indexing articles in PubMed. It ensures consistent retrieval of information by standardizing terminology. MeSH terms are organized hierarchically, from general to specific, and articles are indexed under the most specific headings available. The MeSH database can be searched directly, and suggested terms are provided for any entered search term. MEDLINE Search Searches can be conducted by author, topic, or journal title. Boolean operators (AND, OR, NOT) can refine searches, and limits can be set by language, publication type, date, or abstract availability. Citations often include English abstracts and hyperlinks to related articles. 2. Searching the Internet The internet, particularly the World Wide Web (WWW), is a major source of research information. The WWW connects files via hypertext links and is accessed through browsers like Microsoft Explorer or Netscape Navigator. Websites have addresses called Uniform Resource Locators (URLs), which include components such as the protocol (e.g., http), domain (e.g., .edu for educational institutions), and file type (e.g., .html). Search Engines Search engines allow users to search the content of publicly accessible websites. They vary in functionality, strengths, and weaknesses. Many provide ranked results based on relevance to search terms. Boolean logic and proximity operators (e.g., SAME, WITH) can enhance search specificity. Wildcards (e.g., ) can retrieve variations of a word. Health Information on the Web Health information is one of the most frequently retrieved types of information online. However, the quality of information varies widely. Reliable sources include official websites from reputable organizations, peer-reviewed journals, government institutions, and educational institutions. 3. Free Access to Medical Journals on the Internet The Open Access movement advocates for unrestricted access to research literature. Initiatives like PubMed Central, the Directory of Open Access Journals (DOAJ), and SPARC aim to make scientific and medical literature freely available. These efforts address market dysfunctions in scholarly communication and promote the dissemination of knowledge. 4. Using Journals through HINARI HINARI provides access to journal abstracts for all users, with full-text access available to registered users or institutions subscribing to the journals. Journals can be searched alphabetically by title or by subject.
